name: Victor Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on Ward 9, general medicine, mostly older people with chest infections, falls and heart failure. A day shift starts at seven with handover, then the drug round, which still takes me longer than it should, honestly. I get eight patients if we're fully staffed, ten if we're not, and we're usually not. The bit I love is the washing and the talking, when Mr Okafor in bed four tells me about his allotment. The bit that wears me out is the paperwork on the computer at the end, when my feet are gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the drug round takes longer than it should. What's behind that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I qualified eighteen months ago with a two-year diploma, and I'm still slow. I double-check everything because I failed my IV competency the first time and it shook me. Priya, the charge nurse, is patient with me, but I can see the clock in her eyes. I'd rather be slow than wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly, that's what I'd half expect anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the staff room: the problem on Ward 9 was never computers, it's bodies on the floor. Fix staffing, fix pay, then talk to me about clever software. I'd probably share some union post about it and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. I'm not good with new systems, it took me three months to stop swearing at the e-records screen. But nothing changing also means my rent keeps going up and my pay doesn't, so it's not like everything's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. Keep doing my shifts, keep putting about a hundred a month away, and finally sit my IV competency again in the spring so I stop needing Priya to check me. And stay in the union, because the pay fight is the real fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tired just thinking about the same grind for ten years. Robots aren't what I lie awake about. The rota is what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill hurts most right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent. I share a flat with my cousin Daniel and we got a letter in September saying it's going up another eighty a month each. I've got about three months of costs saved and that letter ate into the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what does a good next year look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Passing that IV competency and getting my confidence back. Maybe moving to the morning-only rota. Honestly, a good year is just being less behind than I am now.

say: The **real problem** on the ward is staffing, not computers.
I'd share the **union line**: fix pay and numbers before buying shiny software.
think: I'm quietly **relieved**, because new systems are hard for me.
Nothing changing still means **rent rises** and flat pay, so life stays tight.
do: Put about **£100 a month** into savings, same as now.
Resit the **IV competency** in the spring.
Stay active in the **union** pay campaign.
feel: **Tired** at the thought of the same grind, more than scared.
S0.quote: Robots aren't what I lie awake about. The rota is what keeps me up.
fieldNote: His worries are **already here**: short staffing, a rent letter and a failed competency.
Relief at no change is mixed with **frustration** about pay that a plateau doesn't fix.
He frames everything through **the union**, even when tech isn't the topic.

steps.text: Resit the IV competency on Ward 9 in the spring
Keep putting about £100 a month into savings
Go to the union branch meetings on the pay claim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the computers get cleverer but people still do the lifting. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the software do the discharge letters and the bed booking, as long as it gives nurses more time with patients and not fewer nurses. I'd be the one at the union meeting asking who decides that. Because I've seen managers say 'time saved' and mean 'post not replaced'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be nervous about being made to use it. I'm the one who still asks our healthcare assistant how to print a wristband, and now they want me talking to an AI. If the charting all moves to some AI voice thing, I'll be the slowest on the ward again. My actual job, washing and turning people, isn't going anywhere soon, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Priya to put me on the training early, even though I'd hate it, so I'm not the last one. I'd push the union branch to get a written agreement that AI time savings go to patient time, not cuts. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more, in case the hospital uses it as an excuse to freeze hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because I think I'll lose my job, the ward's always short. More like being the new kid again who doesn't understand the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the ward would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Sandra. She books transport, chases results, does the discharge paperwork. That's exactly the list on your card. She's been there twenty years and she'd be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go on the training early but you said you'd hate it. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear wins, honestly. I'd hate it more to be the one everyone's covering for. I already know how that feels from the IV thing.

say: I'd welcome AI doing **discharge letters** if it means more patient time.
I'd ask at the union meeting **who decides** where the saved time goes.
think: I'd be the **slowest on the ward** with any new charting system.
My **hands-on work** of washing and turning patients feels safe for now.
do: Sign up early for the **AI charting training**, despite hating it.
Push the branch for a **written agreement** that savings protect staffing.
Save a little more in case of a **hiring freeze**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like being the new kid again on an unfamiliar system.
S1.quote: I'm the one who still asks our healthcare assistant how to print a wristband, and now they want me talking to an AI.
fieldNote: He sees the **ward clerk's job** as the first casualty, not his own.
His fear is **looking incompetent**, rooted in the failed IV competency.
He pairs his own reluctance with a push for **union protections**.

steps.text: Ask the charge nurse for an early place on AI charting training
Push the union branch for a deal protecting ward staffing
Raise monthly savings to about £130 against a hiring freeze

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I've even got good at this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be loud about it. I'd be saying this is exactly why we need the union and why the government has to step in on staffing ratios before any hospital buys a robot. I'd say patients deserve a person, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the computer side of my job is gone by 2028 and I'm not that sad about it. But 2031 scares me. If a robot can wash, turn and do obs as well as I can, then a below-average junior like me is the cheapest thing to cut. I'm not a nurse with twenty years and a specialty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get really serious about money: cut the takeaways, push savings from three months to six. I'd go to every union meeting and I'd write to my MP about safe staffing laws that name humans. And I'd try to get onto a ward that's harder to automate, maybe mental health or end-of-life care, where it's mostly talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. I'd have about three years after the AI arrives before the robots come for the hands-on part, and I'm not sure three years is enough to become good at anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your cousin Daniel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel we might need to keep sharing the flat longer than we planned. He's a warehouse picker, so he'd be in the same boat around 2031. We'd probably just sit there with a beer and not say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to end-of-life care. Would you really, given how you feel about change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it at first. But I'd rather change once, on purpose, than get pushed. Palliative care is still about sitting with people, and I'm better at that than at the clever stuff.

say: Patients **deserve a person**, and the law should say so.
This is why we need the **union** and safe staffing rules now.
think: Losing the **computer work** by 2028 doesn't bother me much.
By **2031** a below-average junior like me is the cheapest thing to cut.
do: Cut takeaways and grow savings from **three to six months**.
Write to my **MP** about safe staffing laws naming humans.
Apply to move into **palliative care**, where talking matters most.
feel: **Scared**, because three years may not be enough to get good at anything.
S2.quote: If a robot can wash, turn and do obs as well as I can, then a below-average junior like me is the cheapest thing to cut.
fieldNote: He separates the **thinking part** of nursing, which he'd let go, from the hands-on part he fears losing.
His **low skill rating** makes him feel first in line, even in a short-staffed profession.
A resistant man still chooses **one deliberate move**, to palliative care, rather than be pushed.

steps.text: Cut takeaways and grow savings to six months of costs
Write to the local MP about safe staffing laws
Apply for a nursing post on a palliative care ward
Attend every union branch meeting on robots and staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as before, just calmer: get the rules in place while there's still time. Five years is enough for unions and governments to write proper staffing laws, so there's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think five years gives me time to stop being the slow one. By 2031 I'd have six years in, maybe a specialty. Then the robots come around 2034, and by 2034 I'd want to be the nurse who supervises the robots, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the IV resit and then a short course in palliative care, paid by the trust if I can wangle it. I'd keep going to the union, and keep savings growing slowly, maybe four months by next year. I wouldn't panic-move, I'd plan it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable sort. Like the night before an exam you've at least started revising for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, which I barely use anyway, and the football subscription. I'd keep the union fees, they're the last thing I'd drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does supervising robots even look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. I picture someone like Priya, checking what the machines did and catching what they missed. I'd need training I don't have, and I'm not sure I'd be picked.

say: Five years leaves **no excuse** for missing staffing laws.
Unions and government should write the **rules now**, while there's time.
think: Five years lets me stop being **the slow one** on the ward.
By **2034** I'd want to supervise the robots, not be replaced by them.
do: Resit the **IV competency**, then a short **palliative course**.
Grow savings slowly toward **four months** of costs.
Keep paying **union fees** above every other cut.
feel: **Anxious**, like the night before an exam you've started revising for.
S3.quote: By 2034 I'd want to be the nurse who supervises the robots, not the one they replace.
fieldNote: The extra years shift him from fear toward a **plan**, though a slow one.
He admits he's unsure he'd be **picked** for supervising roles.
Union fees are the **last cut**, which shows where he puts his trust.

steps.text: Take a short palliative care course funded by the trust
Grow savings to four months by cancelling gym and football
Keep paying union fees and attend staffing meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it to get safe staffing laws and retraining money that actually reaches nurses, not just managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels like real time. I'd be experienced by 2036, and the robots wouldn't be ward-ready until 2039. I'd still worry about what comes after, but I'd be a different nurse by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm doing now, just with a longer horizon. Pass the competency, get a few years in, then maybe do the top-up degree to get my bachelor's by 2030. Keep the union card. Keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. It's a long way off, and I've got bigger problems this year, like my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a top-up degree. Is that real or a someday thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A someday thing, if I'm honest. It costs and I'd need to study around nights. But ten years' warning means I'd finally do the top-up degree instead of calling it a someday thing. I'd probably start by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the trust paid half and gave study days. The union's been asking for that for years. I'd sign up the week it was announced.

say: A decade is time to win **staffing laws** and real retraining money.
Retraining funds must reach **ward nurses**, not just managers.
think: By **2036** I'd be experienced, and robots wouldn't reach wards until 2039.
My **rent** is a bigger problem this year than robots.
do: Pass the competency and build **a few years** on the ward.
Plan a **top-up degree** to finish by about 2030.
Keep the **union card** and keep saving monthly.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, because it feels a long way off.
S4.quote: Ten years' warning means I'd finally do the top-up degree instead of calling it a someday thing.
fieldNote: Time **softens** him a lot, from anxious to uneasy.
His plans depend on the **trust paying**, which ties back to union demands.
Even in the slow version, his **rent** stays the pressing worry.

steps.text: Keep working on Ward 9 and build experience
Start a part-time nursing top-up degree by 2029
Back the union claim for trust-paid study days

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years for the computers and then three for the robots is just not enough for someone like me who's still learning. What would help is a law that says a ward needs a set number of human nurses, and the trust paying for us to retrain into the parts of care that are about people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients. Mr Okafor doesn't want a robot washing him, and I don't think anyone's asked the patients. Ten years with a better chance of a top-up degree would be lovely, but asking the patients would matter more.

headlineQuote: Mr Okafor doesn't want a robot washing him, and I don't think anyone's asked the patients.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old junior nurse** on a general medical ward, still rebuilding confidence after failing a competency.
He shares a flat with his cousin and has about **three months saved**, squeezed by a rent rise.
He dislikes new tech and leans on **the union** for answers to every change.
His mood rises to **anxious** only when robots look able to replace hands-on care within a few years.
With more warning he'd move toward **palliative care** or a top-up degree, rather than wait to be pushed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years before robots isn't enough time to get good at anything.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing law** requiring a set number of human nurses per ward.
**Trust-paid retraining** into the people-centred parts of care.
